title: 1LongForcing extends teacher guidance over student rollouts. Qualitative snapshots from the 5B interactive model span stress-test rollouts sampled up to 24 hours.

paper.title: 1LongForcing extends teacher guidance over student rollouts. Qualitative snapshots from the 5B interactive model span stress-test rollouts sampled up to 24 hours.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: “We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.” — Alan Turing Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models are becoming a foundational paradigm for long-horizon world rollout. An AR model generates video chunk by chunk, with each new chunk conditioned on previously generated frames. Repeating this process enables rollouts far longer than individual training clips. This capability is essential for both interactive world models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , where a world must remain coherent and responsive as the user acts, and long-form text-to-video systems [ 7 , 8 ] , where visual quality, motion, and identity must persist far beyond the initial clip. However, the same recursive mechanism that enables long rollouts also makes AR models vulnerable to rollout drift . Because every generated chunk becomes context for the next, small errors compound, the conditioning distribution moves away from the data seen during training, and the model gradually loses visual fidelity. Modern real-time AR video generators are often obtained through a three-stage distillation pipeline. Teacher forcing first adapts a bidirectional video model to causal conditioning, ODE distillation compresses its denoising trajectory into a few-step generator, and distribution matching distillation (DMD) aligns the student’s self-generated distribution with a teacher [ 9 , 8 , 10 ] . This recipe is highly effective within the few-second horizon on which it is trained, but deployment requires closed-loop generation over minutes. Teacher forcing learns from short clean histories, causal ODE distillation uses short teacher-generated trajectories, and short-horizon DMD evaluates only short student rollouts; later rollout states receive no direct supervision from this objective. Recent approaches mitigate long-horizon drift through sparse local matching [ 11 ] , inference-time memory and positional modifications [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , or context perturbation [ 15 ] . Local matching can supervise late rollout states, but its jointly scored windows remain short; inference-time modifications instead stabilize the conditioning context. Neither mechanism by itself matches the longer joint path, leaving cross-window dependencies that can affect visual fidelity, identity, dynamics, and action consistency. These failures reveal a supervision-horizon gap between short-window training and long-horizon deployment. Our principle is that temporal manifold matching should scale with the trajectories visited on policy , where temporal manifold informally describes high-probability regions of the teacher’s path distribution. Section 4 formalizes this view using path distributions, KL divergence, and total variation. Matching short windows does not determine the distribution of a long rollout, whereas matching clean trajectories controls drift within the supervised horizon. Beyond this horizon, stability also depends on teacher leakage, student–teacher mismatch along visited states, and recovery from drifted states. This motivates extending distribution matching over longer student rollouts while keeping teacher forcing and ODE distillation short. Guided by this principle, we introduce LongForcing , which replaces Causal Forcing’s DMD real-score teacher with an extended-horizon teacher for longer self-generated trajectories. The student rolls out on policy, while an extended-horizon teacher supplies distribution-level supervision across a long, contiguous portion of each self-generated training trajectory, requiring no architectural changes. Empirically, LongForcing improves text-to-video VBench Quality by 0.93 points over Causal Forcing and raises WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points (37% relative) in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours . These results position temporal manifold matching at scale as a practical step toward long-horizon world models. Our contributions are threefold: • We formalize the supervision-horizon gap : longer student rollouts expose delayed failures, and joint path matching constrains dependencies left undetermined by local-window marginals. • We introduce LongForcing , which extends the teacher’s supervision horizon in distribution-matching distillation to guide longer student-generated trajectories. • We evaluate LongForcing across interactive world models and text-to-video generation, measuring improvements in action following and video quality alongside their dependence on supervision length.

sections.heading: 2.1  Autoregressive Long-Video Generation
sections.text: Autoregressive video generation has evolved from discrete-token transformers [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] to diffusion and flow models that stream through temporally varying noise levels, causal attention, or sliding-window denoising [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Few-step variants further use video DMD, student-generated contexts, progressive-window denoising, corrected causal ODE initialization, or diagonal distillation [ 9 , 8 , 25 , 10 , 26 ] . To extend generation beyond the training horizon, training-free methods modify noise schedules, denoising windows, attention, positional encodings, or temporal memory [ 27 , 7 , 13 , 14 , 28 , 29 ] , whereas training-based approaches use self-generated segments, long-context tuning, hierarchical denoising, and drift simulation [ 11 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] . Context Forcing [ 31 ] also uses a long-context teacher, combining continuation-conditioned DMD with Slow-Fast Memory. LongForcing retains Causal Forcing’s student architecture and inference procedure, replacing its DMD teacher to score a longer contiguous, jointly noised student path.

sections.heading: 2.2  Interactive World Models
sections.text: Interactive world models use video generation as a controllable simulator for prediction, exploration, and closed-loop interaction. Recent systems demonstrate playable game simulation [ 3 , 4 , 34 ] , camera and action-controlled world exploration [ 5 , 35 , 6 ] , and real-time interactive generation [ 2 , 36 , 37 ] . Unlike prompt-driven video generation, interactive rollout must preserve both world state and the consequences of continuously changing user actions. Over extended sessions, accumulated errors can therefore degrade not only visual fidelity and identity, but also action responsiveness and physical consistency. WorldRoamBench [ 38 ] explicitly evaluates these long-horizon properties across diverse interactive environments. LongForcing scales teacher supervision of on-policy rollouts along the temporal axis in both interactive and text-conditioned generation. Qualitative stress tests sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours , complementing the benchmark evaluation. Figure 2: Visual and feature-space signatures of rollout drift. sections.text: An efficient causal student is typically obtained through teacher forcing on short clean histories, causal ODE distillation into a few-step generator, and DMD refinement [ 10 , 40 , 41 ] . DMD compares bidirectional real and fake scores on student-generated closed-loop paths; Self Forcing [ 8 ] applies this refinement on policy, but only within a short rollout window.

sections.heading: 5  LongForcing
sections.text: LongForcing builds on Causal Forcing [ 10 ] . We retain its short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, and replace the real-score teacher in the final asymmetric DMD stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. This teacher supervises longer student self-rollouts using the standard DMD formulation, motivated by the analysis in Section 4 .

As in asymmetric DMD, the student generates causally and both score networks evaluate its noised path bidirectionally. The longer scoring horizon covers later prefixes; Appendix A.2 – A.4 gives the objective’s scope and score estimator.

sections.heading: Extended-horizon teacher.
sections.text: The frozen real-score model is trained or fine-tuned on long sequences so that it can score the complete H H -step path; the online fake-score model uses the same long bidirectional context to track the current student distribution. For interactive training, a pre-specified action plan is supplied over the same horizon. The extended horizon increases supervision coverage; the guarantees remain conditional on teacher quality and student–teacher mismatch.

sections.heading: Interactive world model.
sections.text: We train action-conditioned models on Wan2.2-5B [ 42 ] and Wan2.1-1.3B [ 43 ] and evaluate 60-second WorldRoamBench rollouts: third-person for the 5B comparison and first-person for the 1.3B horizon ablation. Teacher forcing and ODE distillation use 121 and 81 frames for the 5B and 1.3B models, respectively, while DMD extends both to 321 frames. DMD training uses AdamW on eight GPUs with a global batch size of 8 for 1000 steps. The generator and fake-score network use constant learning rates of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} and 4 × 10 − 7 4\times 10^{-7} , respectively, with ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0,0.999) and weight decay 0.01 0.01 .

sections.heading: Text-to-video model.
sections.text: For text-to-video, we follow Causal Forcing [ 10 ] on Wan2.1-1.3B [ 43 ] at 832 × 480 832{\times}480 resolution. We retain its teacher-forcing and causal ODE configurations, replace the DMD real-score teacher, and use 321-frame DMD rollouts. DMD uses AdamW on 8 GPUs with a global batch size of 8 and learning rates of 2 × 10 − 6 2{\times}10^{-6} and 4 × 10 − 7 4{\times}10^{-7} for the generator and fake-score network. We evaluate with the official 5-second VBench protocol [ 44 ] and VBench-Long [ 45 ] on 30-second generations. See Appendix A.1 for further details.

sections.text: Figure 3 shows how text-to-video generation deteriorates as rollouts grow longer. Extending supervision from 81 to 321 frames reduces the mean drift score at 59 seconds from 67.46 to 31.91, a relative reduction of 52.7%. The gap between the curves grows over time, indicating that longer supervision slows error accumulation and helps maintain quality during extended generation, although some drift remains. sections.heading: Human study.
sections.text: Across 400 judgments per criterion from 20 evaluators on 20 shared cases, 321-frame LongForcing receives 72.0% overall preference, compared with 16.2% for the 81-frame model and 11.8% ties (Figure 3 ). Preferences also favor longer supervision in visual quality by 71.2% to 13.8%, temporal coherence by 67.0% to 18.2%, and motion naturalness by 64.8% to 17.8%. Appendix C.4 gives the evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: 7  Conclusion
sections.text: We identify a supervision-horizon gap in autoregressive video generation: short-horizon supervision leaves later rollout behavior underdetermined, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to teacher guidance. LongForcing addresses this gap by replacing Causal Forcing’s DMD real-score teacher with an extended-horizon teacher that supervises longer student self-rollouts, while retaining its short teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages. Across text-to-video generation and interactive world models, this improves VBench Quality by 0.93 points and first-person action score by 23.9 points over the respective baselines, without changing the architecture or increasing inference cost. Horizon ablations and time-resolved evaluations show reduced rollout drift, complemented by qualitative interactive stress tests sampled up to 24 hours. These findings position temporal supervision as a scaling dimension for video world models. Integrating coherent visual rollouts with persistent memory and hierarchical planning offers a path toward persistent interactive worlds, goal-directed behavior, and long-term reasoning.

sections.heading: A.1  Training Pipeline
sections.text: LongForcing retains the teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages of Causal Forcing and replaces the real-score teacher in its final DMD stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. Teacher forcing uses short clean histories and causal ODE distillation uses short trajectories from the causal teacher; the resulting student generates a contiguous H H -chunk closed-loop path, scored jointly by the replacement teacher and the online fake-score network. The student architecture, sampler, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Under the causal VAE mapping, 81, 161, 241, and 321 decoded RGB frames correspond to 21, 41, 61, and 81 temporal latent positions, respectively; these positions are rounded and grouped into autoregressive chunks of three latent frames.

sections.heading: Interactive teacher: initialization and data.
sections.text: The interactive teachers use the pretrained Wan2.2-5B and Wan2.1-1.3B backbones, adapted to action-conditioned video generation on the ABot-World training data [ 49 ] . We train the interactive teachers for 20,000 steps with a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} and a global batch size of 256 video clips. We use action-annotated video sequences, with the action sequence aligned to the video over the teacher’s temporal window. The teacher retains bidirectional temporal attention so that it can evaluate the complete student-generated path with its corresponding actions. The data collection and annotation pipeline is described in ABot-World [ 49 ] ; the long teacher provides the frozen real-score network for our 321-frame DMD stage.

sections.heading: Text-to-video teacher: long-video adaptation.
sections.text: We initialize the bidirectional teacher from the pretrained Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B checkpoint [ 43 ] and fine-tune it on UltraVideo-Long [ 50 ] for three epochs, with each training example visited once per epoch. Videos are sampled at 16 FPS and processed at 832 × 480 832\times 480 resolution, using 321-frame clips for the long teacher. The horizon study uses separate teacher checkpoints for the 81-, 161-, 241-, and 321-frame DMD configurations, pairing each rollout length with its corresponding teacher. The pretrained Wan VAE and UMT5 text encoder remain frozen; video latents and text embeddings are cached before optimization. We optimize a supervised flow-matching loss on the noisy video latents, sampling a diffusion timestep and Gaussian noise anew for each example and applying the scheduler’s timestep-dependent loss weight. Adaptation uses rank-64 LoRA with scaling parameter α = 64 \alpha=64 in the DiT attention projections ( q,k,v,o ) and feed-forward projections ( ffn.0,ffn.2 ); the underlying pretrained weights remain frozen. AdamW uses a base learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.01 0.01 , and its default momentum parameters ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (0.9,0.999) . The implementation uses BF16 model parameters, evaluates the mean-squared-error loss in FP32, enables gradient checkpointing, and processes one clip per GPU without gradient accumulation, giving a global batch size of 32 clips. After adaptation, the resulting teacher is frozen during DMD; only the causal generator and the online fake-score network are updated in that stage.

sections.heading: Resources and DMD configuration.
sections.text: We follow Causal Forcing [ 10 ] for DMD timestep sampling and loss weighting. LongForcing extends the real-score teacher’s supervision horizon and the student rollout length. Interactive teacher training uses 256 GPUs, while text-to-video teacher training uses 32 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The subsequent DMD stage runs for 1,000 global steps on eight GPUs with a global batch size of eight trajectories in both text-to-video and interactive experiments. The generator and fake-score learning rates are 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} and 4 × 10 − 7 4\times 10^{-7} , respectively, with AdamW momentum parameters ( 0 , 0.999 ) (0,0.999) and weight decay 0.01 0.01 . For text-to-video DMD training, the fake-score network is updated at every global step, whereas the generator is updated once every five global steps, giving a 5 : 1 5{:}1 ratio of fake-score to generator updates. For both the 1.3B and 5B interactive world models, the fake-score network is updated at every global step and the generator once every three global steps during DMD training.

sections.heading: When does LongForcing help?
sections.text: Horizon scaling targets failures first reached beyond the shorter training window. Extending the on-policy rollout makes these later prefixes available to the teacher, while the horizon ablations quantify the resulting empirical changes in generation quality. The benefit depends on both supervision coverage and the quality of the teacher signal on those prefixes.

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: The additional computation occurs during training: the student generates longer paths and both score networks process longer sequences. At fixed spatial resolution, dense bidirectional attention has quadratic attention-score computation in temporal length; practical memory and runtime depend on the attention and gradient implementations. For a fixed inference configuration and output length, the student uses the same architecture and sampling operations as the short-horizon baseline.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: The finite-horizon results quantify teacher-relative path agreement, while the blockwise extension additionally assumes controlled leakage, mismatch, and recovery on the student’s start distribution. The long-run extension states its uniform dynamical assumptions separately. These conditions concern the specified model, domain, and action protocol. Visual quality, motion, and action following are evaluated separately, complementing the drift analysis.

sections.heading: How long is enough?
sections.text: A useful supervision horizon depends on when task-relevant dependencies and failure modes become observable, rather than on a universal duration. For scene roaming, delayed effects may involve revisiting a location or maintaining an object after a long absence; for goal-directed interaction, an action’s consequence may appear much later. Our horizon sweep measures the benefit of extending supervision within the tested range; determining a sufficient horizon for a new task calls for evaluating those dependencies over the intended deployment duration. A promising direction is to allocate longer training rollouts when delayed errors remain frequent, and to compare this adaptive allocation with fixed horizons under matched compute budgets. Teacher quality and persistent memory offer complementary ways to make additional temporal coverage useful.

sections.heading: From visual rollout to long-term planning.
sections.text: Maintaining a coherent visual trajectory and deciding which events should occur over a long story or task are complementary problems. LongForcing strengthens the former by supervising longer self-generated paths; long-term planning additionally requires representing goals, organizing events, and retaining consequences across distant steps. This suggests a hierarchical approach in which a planner maintains an abstract state and selects subgoals, persistent memory records relevant past events, and a video model renders the resulting interactions. Long-horizon supervision could then assess whether the rendered trajectory respects those plans and remembered consequences. Evaluating delayed action effects, goal completion, and narrative consistency alongside visual quality would help determine whether longer rollouts also support more coherent long-term behavior.

Abstract Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap : short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing , a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the real-score teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours , far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. Qualitative snapshots from the 5B interactive model span stress-test rollouts sampled up to 24 hours . 1 Introduction “We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.” — Alan Turing Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models are becoming a foundational paradigm for long-horizon world rollout. An AR model generates video chunk by chunk, with each new chunk conditioned on previously generated frames. Repeating this process enables rollouts far longer than individual training clips. This capability is essential for both interactive world models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , where a world must remain coherent and responsive as the user acts, and long-form text-to-video systems [ 7 , 8 ] , where visual quality, motion, and identity must persist far beyond the initial clip. However, the same recursive mechanism that enables long rollouts also makes AR models vulnerable to rollout drift . Because every generated chunk becomes context for the next, small errors compound, the conditioning distribution moves away from the data seen during training, and the model gradually loses visual fidelity. Modern real-time AR video generators are often obtained through a three-stage distillation pipeline. Teacher forcing first adapts a bidirectional video model to causal conditioning, ODE distillation compresses its denoising trajectory into a few-step generator, and distribution matching distillation (DMD) aligns the student’s self-generated distribution with a teacher [ 9 , 8 , 10 ] . This recipe is highly effective within the few-second horizon on which it is trained, but deployment requires closed-loop generation over minutes. Teacher forcing learns from short clean histories, causal ODE distillation uses short teacher-generated trajectories, and short-horizon DMD evaluates only short student rollouts; later rollout states receive no direct supervision from this objective. Recent approaches mitigate long-horizon drift through sparse local matching [ 11 ] , inference-time memory and positional modifications [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , or context perturbation [ 15 ] . Local matching can supervise late rollout states, but its jointly scored windows remain short; inference-time modifications instead stabilize the conditioning context. Neither mechanism by itself matches the longer joint path, leaving cross-window dependencies that can affect visual fidelity, identity, dynamics, and action consistency. These failures reveal a supervision-horizon gap between short-window training and long-horizon deployment. Our principle is that temporal manifold matching should scale with the trajectories visited on policy , where temporal manifold informally describes high-probability regions of the teacher’s path distribution. Section 4 formalizes this view using path distributions, KL divergence, and total variation. Matching short windows does not determine the distribution of a long rollout, whereas matching clean trajectories controls drift within the supervised horizon. Beyond this horizon, stability also depends on teacher leakage, student–teacher mismatch along visited states, and recovery from drifted states. This motivates extending distribution matching over longer student rollouts while keeping teacher forcing and ODE distillation short. Guided by this principle, we introduce LongForcing , which replaces Causal Forcing’s DMD real-score teacher with an extended-horizon teacher for longer self-generated trajectories. The student rolls out on policy, while an extended-horizon teacher supplies distribution-level supervision across a long, contiguous portion of each self-generated training trajectory, requiring no architectural changes. Empirically, LongForcing improves text-to-video VBench Quality by 0.93 points over Causal Forcing and raises WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points (37% relative) in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours . These results position temporal manifold matching at scale as a practical step toward long-horizon world models. Our contributions are threefold: • We formalize the supervision-horizon gap : longer student rollouts expose delayed failures, and joint path matching constrains dependencies left undetermined by local-window marginals. • We introduce LongForcing , which extends the teacher’s supervision horizon in distribution-matching distillation to guide longer student-generated trajectories. • We evaluate LongForcing across interactive world models and text-to-video generation, measuring improvements in action following and video quality alongside their dependence on supervision length. 2 Related Work 2.1 Autoregressive Long-Video Generation Autoregressive video generation has evolved from discrete-token transformers [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] to diffusion and flow models that stream through temporally varying noise levels, causal attention, or sliding-window denoising [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Few-step variants further use video DMD, student-generated contexts, progressive-window denoising, corrected causal ODE initialization, or diagonal distillation [ 9 , 8 , 25 , 10 , 26 ] . To extend generation beyond the training horizon, training-free methods modify noise schedules, denoising windows, attention, positional encodings, or temporal memory [ 27 , 7 , 13 , 14 , 28 , 29 ] , whereas training-based approaches use self-generated segments, long-context tuning, hierarchical denoising, and drift simulation [ 11 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] . Context Forcing [ 31 ] also uses a long-context teacher, combining continuation-conditioned DMD with Slow-Fast Memory. LongForcing retains Causal Forcing’s student architecture and inference procedure, replacing its DMD teacher to score a longer contiguous, jointly noised student path. 2.2 Interactive World Models Interactive world models use video generation as a controllable simulator for prediction, exploration, and closed-loop interaction. Recent systems demonstrate playable game simulation [ 3 , 4 , 34 ] , camera and action-controlled world exploration [ 5 , 35 , 6 ] , and real-time interactive generation [ 2 , 36 , 37 ] . Unlike prompt-driven video generation, interactive rollout must preserve both world state and the consequences of continuously changing user actions. Over extended sessions, accumulated errors can therefore degrade not only visual fidelity and identity, but also action responsiveness and physical consistency. WorldRoamBench [ 38 ] explicitly evaluates these long-horizon properties across diverse interactive environments. LongForcing scales teacher supervision of on-policy rollouts along the temporal axis in both interactive and text-conditioned generation. Qualitative stress tests sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours , complementing the benchmark evaluation. Figure 2: Visual and feature-space signatures of rollout drift. LongForcing addresses this gap by replacing Causal Forcing’s DMD real-score teacher with an extended-horizon teacher that supervises longer student self-rollouts, while retaining its short teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages. Across text-to-video generation and interactive world models, this improves VBench Quality by 0.93 points and first-person action score by 23.9 points over the respective baselines, without changing the architecture or increasing inference cost. Horizon ablations and time-resolved evaluations show reduced rollout drift, complemented by qualitative interactive stress tests sampled up to 24 hours. These findings position temporal supervision as a scaling dimension for video world models. Integrating coherent visual rollouts with persistent memory and hierarchical planning offers a path toward persistent interactive worlds, goal-directed behavior, and long-term reasoning.
